--- title: "Comparing campaigns" --- The grid from [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd) holds five campaigns run against one baseline. The policy question is which net to buy, and the frame does not answer it directly. It gives five rows and twenty-three columns, and the answer depends on which column the arms are ranked on. A column that summarises the horizon badly gives a different ordering of the products from one that summarises it well. Rebuilding it takes the same district dictionary and the same five `Scenario` objects. ::: {#1aa00c88 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget district = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, py_only=0.70, routine=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), ) grid = [ Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district), Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district), Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district), ] res = run_scenarios(grid) ``` ::: And recover the time grid from the emulator's own configuration. ::: {#994e9513 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} _, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] window = cfg["window_size"] abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + window * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365 idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]))) idx_y9 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 78 ``` ::: ::: ## Ranking on endline prevalence Endline prevalence is the simplest comparison, and `prev_endline` is prevalence in the final 14-day window, three years after the campaign. Sort ascending and put the change from `prev_y9` beside it. ::: {#5377166f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_prevalence = ( res[["name", "prev_y9", "prev_endline"]] .assign(change=lambda d: d["prev_endline"] - d["prev_y9"]) .sort_values("prev_endline") .reset_index(drop=True) ) by_prevalence.round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
name prev_y9 prev_endline change
0 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.456 0.0381 -0.4179
1 Pyrrole 0.456 0.4642 0.0082
2 PBO 0.456 0.4701 0.0141
3 Pyrethroid-only 0.456 0.4837 0.0277
4 Withdraw 0.456 0.4981 0.0421
``` ::: ::: The order follows `dn0_future`, with pyrrole ranking ahead of PBO, PBO ahead of pyrethroid-only, and pyrethroid-only ahead of no campaign, while the combination arm ranks well ahead of all three. In the `change` column, only the combination arm ends *below* where it started; every net-only arm ends higher than prevalence at the campaign, because endline sits three years after distribution, by which time all three products are at their least effective. The three net products are separated by under two prevalence points at endline, which is not much on which to spend a procurement budget. ## Ranking on endline cases Ranking on `cases_endline` rather than on prevalence produces a different order, and a surprising one. ::: {#71187a3b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_cases = ( res[["name", "cases_endline"]] .sort_values("cases_endline") .reset_index(drop=True) ) by_cases.round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
name cases_endline
0 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.1653
1 Withdraw 2.1272
2 Pyrrole 2.3899
3 PBO 2.4124
4 Pyrethroid-only 2.4331
``` ::: ::: Withdrawing the nets now appears as the second-best option, ahead of any of the three products the district might actually buy, which is an artefact of the summary column rather than anything the campaigns did. The two rankings disagree because `cases_endline` is a poor summary of the horizon. ::: {.callout-note} ## Endline is a point, and cases are not monotone in prevalence `cases_endline` is clinical incidence in a single 14-day window three years after the campaign, and two things go wrong with it, since the window is noisy (the incidence series oscillates from one fortnight to the next) and clinical incidence is not a monotone function of transmission. The withdrawal arm has spent three years at higher prevalence, and the simulator's immunity dynamics carry that through into fewer clinical episodes per person late in the horizon. Rank campaigns on the integrated cases series rather than on a single window of it. ::: ## Trajectories The figure below shows both panels and all five arms, with the dashed line marking the campaign. ::: {#b309cb01 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(7.2, 6.6)) for _, row in res.iterrows(): axes[0].plot(years, np.asarray(row["prevalence"]), label=row["name"]) axes[1].plot(years, np.asarray(row["cases"]), label=row["name"]) for ax in axes: ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_ylim(0, None) axes[0].set_ylabel("Prevalence (under 5)") axes[0].legend(ncol=2) axes[1].set_ylabel("Clinical incidence") axes[1].set_xlabel("Years since campaign") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Prevalence and clinical incidence under five candidate campaigns, from three years before the campaign to three years after. All five arms are identical until the dashed line.](comparing_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two stacked line charts sharing an x-axis in years since the campaign. The upper panel shows under-five prevalence for five scenarios: all overlap before the campaign at around 0.45, then diverge. Withdrawal climbs to about 0.50; pyrethroid-only, PBO and pyrrole dip and rebound to between 0.46 and 0.48; the PBO plus IRS plus LSM arm falls to below 0.05 and stays there. The lower panel shows clinical incidence, with the same ordering and a visible oscillation from window to window.'} ::: ::: The five lines coincide until the campaign, after which the three net arms reduce prevalence, reach a minimum roughly a year in, and converge back towards each other as their insecticide decays. The withdrawal arm rises throughout the post-campaign period, while the combination arm falls well below the other four and remains there, because IRS and LSM do not decay on the same three-year clock as a net. The lower panel shows why the endline point is unreliable. The incidence series oscillates from one window to the next, and by the right-hand edge the net arms have converged into a band that overlaps the withdrawal arm. The final window carries no information about the three years in between, over which the benefit of the campaign accrues. ## Cases averted The decision turns on the total clinical burden over the years the campaign is meant to cover. That is the area under the incidence curve from the campaign to the end of the horizon. Integrate `cases` from `idx_y9` onwards, with the timestep expressed in years. ::: {#9505b9eb .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} step_years = window / 365 burden = pd.Series( { row["name"]: float(np.trapezoid(np.asarray(row["cases"])[idx_y9:], dx=step_years)) for _, row in res.iterrows() }, name="burden", ) burden.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` Withdraw 7.577 Pyrethroid-only 5.619 PBO 4.815 Pyrrole 4.548 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.295 Name: burden, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: `cases` is reported on the emulator's own incidence scale, and because every arm shares that scale, differences and percentages between arms are meaningful without pinning the units. The counterfactual is the withdrawal arm. ::: {#13c37d3b .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} baseline = burden["Withdraw"] averted = ( pd.DataFrame( { "burden": burden, "averted": baseline - burden, "averted_pct": 100 * (baseline - burden) / baseline, } ) .sort_values("averted", ascending=False) .rename_axis("campaign") ) averted.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
burden averted averted_pct
campaign
PBO + IRS + LSM 0.29 7.28 96.11
Pyrrole 4.55 3.03 39.98
PBO 4.81 2.76 36.46
Pyrethroid-only 5.62 1.96 25.85
Withdraw 7.58 0.00 0.00
``` ::: ::: ::: {#802bc911 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} bars = averted.drop(index="Withdraw").sort_values("averted_pct") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4)) ax.barh(bars.index, bars["averted_pct"], height=0.55) ax.set_axisbelow(True) ax.set_xlabel("Clinical burden averted vs withdrawal (%)") ax.set_xlim(0, 100) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Post-campaign clinical burden averted relative to withdrawing the nets, integrated over the three years after the campaign.](comparing_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of percentage of clinical burden averted relative to net withdrawal. PBO plus IRS plus LSM averts about 96 per cent, pyrrole about 40 per cent, PBO about 36 per cent, and pyrethroid-only about 26 per cent.'} ::: ::: ## Which net to buy The three net-only arms are separated by under two prevalence points at endline. Over the three years the nets are in the field they are separated by fourteen percentage points of averted burden, with pyrethroid-only averting about a quarter of the burden that withdrawing the nets would incur, PBO about a third, and pyrrole about two fifths. None of that is visible in an endline column. The ordering follows `dn0_future` and nothing else, so it is only as good as the resistance level supplied. At resistance 0.30 the difference between a pyrethroid-only net and a pyrrole net is substantial; at resistance 0.0 it is much smaller, and the cheaper net becomes a reasonable choice. The resistance estimate has error bars, so re-run the grid across its plausible range before committing to a product. The combination arm averts almost all of the burden, at a cost the emulator does not represent. ## Next - [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) — get these tables and trajectories out of Python. - [Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) — how `res_use` sets the ordering. - [EIR, HBR, prevalence, and cases](../03-concepts/equilibrium.qmd) — why cases are not monotone in transmission.
